title: China, U.S. allies push back on latest round of White House tariffs
summary: China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by Donald Trump's administration and hit back at allegations they have excess manufacturing capacity.

image.caption: A container ship sits in front of the Manhattan skyline as seen from Bayonne, N.J., on Tuesday. Donald Trump has hailed the revenue from tariffs on imported goods, but they've proven unpopular with American voters while serving as a source of frustration for U.S. allies. (Seth Wenig/The Associated P

blocks.text: World
China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by Donald Trump's administration and hit back at allegations they have excess manufacturing capacity.
Overseas markets appear to have been prepared for latest round of White House tariffs

The new tariffs, which are likely to take effect early next year, were announced Wednesday. They are intended to help reinstate tariffs for most of the economies after the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in February struck down most of Trump's sweeping tariffs implemented last year.

The new import duties followed a monthslong Section 301 probe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he determined that practices of the 14 economies relating to excess capacity and production in manufacturing are "unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce."

Stock markets in Europe and Asia posted solid gains on Thursday as the latest salvo of tariffs looked less damaging than first feared. The new rates are also unlikely to be imposed until February or March.
"The macro impact from this increase is likely to be modest, particularly given the fact that the investigations have been telegraphed well in advance," said analysts at JPMorgan.
"Several key imports are still exempt from tariffs, including tech goods, and the administration has shown itself to be sensitive to market disruptions," they added.

blocks.text: Stocks in Europe gained 1.6 per cent in early trading, following on from gains across Asia.
Wall Street is closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday,
'Republicans have learned nothing': House Democrat
Canada was not subjected to the new tariffs. While Trump and Greer have raised a number of objections to what it portrays as unfair trade practices from Ottawa, excess capacity was not one of them.
Trump himself made no public remarks on the new actions, a marked contrast with his "Liberation Day" tariff announcement in April 2025 in the White House Rose Garden.
Canada spared from new U.S. tariffs, but gaps remain in trade talks

Trump has hailed the revenue that tariffs bring to the U.S. government, but the protectionist policies are unpopular with voters, who associate them with higher prices on many consumer goods, according to several polls. Republicans in Congress were quick to blame the president’s tariff policy for the party's stunning midterm losses earlier this month.
Several Democrats have argued that, by punishing allies, the policy did little to actual aggressive trade practices from Beijing.
"Republicans have learned nothing," incoming House Majority Leader Katherine Clark of Massachusetts said on X.
China calls tariffs 'pretext for political manouevring'
China, one of the biggest trading partners of the U.S., is facing a 20 per cent tariff. It slammed the notion of "overcapacity" as a "false premise."
"China opposes its use as a pretext for political manouevring," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said at a regular press briefing.

China's commerce ministry urged the U.S. to "correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation." Ministry spokesperson He Yadong also said China reserves the rights to retaliate to the measures if necessary.

The U.S. and China have extended by two months a trade truce that's set to expire on Jan. 10. The two countries also have agreed on tariff cuts on reciprocal lists of non-sensitive products worth about $60 billion.

Japan faces new U.S. tariffs of up to 15 per cent, matching the ceiling agreed in last year's trade talks in exchange for its commitment to invest $550 billion in the United States. The Japanese government said it protested to Washington.
"Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a regular news conference Thursday.
Follows 'forced labour' tariffs

Malaysia said it "does not have excess capacity in its manufacturing sectors that distorts or disrupts global markets," adding that it will continue to engage and consult with the United States. Malaysia said it will continue consultations with the United States to ensure total tariffs do not exceed 19 per cent, as it was one of the first nations to sign a trade pact with Washington.

On Wednesday, the European Commission expects any measures imposed by Washington needed to respect the previously negotiated 15 per cent tariff ceiling for EU goods imports. A spokesperson for the commission said it strongly rejected the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity.

blocks.text: Analysts say the 14 economies targeted by the Trump administration together account for roughly half of the global economy.

The latest U.S. tariffs are not as alarming as they look, said Stephen Brown, a chief economist with Capital Economics, as they are essentially broadly replacing, rather than adding to, earlier announced U.S. tariffs related to forced labour allegations announced in July.
Still, the new tariffs will likely help push prices higher and may "keep core goods inflation firm into next year," he said in a commentary.
